lines.text: Painters, sculptors, bankers and thinkers who looked back to Rome and Greece, and remade Europe in the process. This is the Renaissance, from Giotto to Shakespeare.
It starts in Tuscany with Giotto, whose frescoes gave painted people weight and feeling. Later artists saw him as the one who began it all.
At the end of the thirteenth century, Florence began a vast new cathedral. Its dome would wait more than a century for a man bold enough to build it.
The poet Petrarch hunted for lost Latin manuscripts and wrote sonnets to his beloved Laura, lighting the spark of a new learning.
From the Italian cities, a rebirth was under way, a fresh hunger for ancient learning and new ideas in art, science and writing.
Its heart was humanism, the study of Greek and Roman writers, and a belief in what people and their cities could achieve.
In the wake of the Black Death, Boccaccio wrote The Decameron, a hundred tales told by young Florentines sheltering from the plague.
Then came Brunelleschi. He worked out how to raise the cathedral's dome without the usual wooden frame, and he found the rules of linear perspective.
His friend Donatello cast a bronze David, the first free-standing nude statue since ancient times.
Behind the scenes, the banker Cosimo de' Medici ran Florence and paid for its buildings, artists and scholars.
Far to the north, in the Low Countries, Jan van Eyck was perfecting oil paint, catching fur, jewels and light in astonishing detail.
The Medici family's bank would make them masters of Florence for generations, and the greatest patrons of the age.
In Germany, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg would soon change how ideas travelled.
Back in Florence, the young Masaccio painted frescoes with true perspective and real light, before dying in his twenties.
Piero della Francesca, painter and mathematician, made calm, geometric pictures and wrote about perspective itself.
In 1432 the van Eyck brothers finished the Ghent Altarpiece, a landmark of oil painting that has since been stolen and hidden more than once.
Meanwhile Gutenberg's printing press made books cheap, and the new ideas could spread across Europe faster than ever before.
In Rome, the future warrior pope Julius the Second was born. He would set Michelangelo and Raphael to their greatest work.
Sandro Botticelli painted for the Medici with flowing, graceful lines, then was all but forgotten for centuries.
Under Lorenzo the Magnificent, Florence reached the height of its glory, with Botticelli and the young Michelangelo in his circle.
In 1452 Leonardo da Vinci was born near Florence: painter, engineer and endlessly curious student of nature.
The same year saw the birth of Savonarola, the friar who would thunder against luxury, rule Florence for a time, and die at the stake.
In 1453 the Ottomans took Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire came to an end.
In the north, Erasmus became the leading humanist of his age, printing the Greek New Testament and calling for reform of the Church.
In Florence, Machiavelli would study how rulers really win and keep power, and his name became a byword.
In Nuremberg, Albrecht Durer carried Italian ideas north of the Alps, and his engravings spread through the new print trade.
In Poland, Nicolaus Copernicus would argue that the Earth moves around the Sun, overturning the old picture of the heavens.
And in 1475 Michelangelo was born, sculptor, painter and architect, who would carve, paint and build some of the age's greatest works.
The same year brought Cesare Borgia, a pope's son who carved out a state by war and murder, and a model for Machiavelli's prince.
Around 1480 Botticelli painted Primavera, a spring garden full of gods and nymphs.
Raphael was born, the painter whose balance and grace would become the model for centuries, though he died at thirty-seven.
Botticelli's Birth of Venus brought the goddess ashore on a seashell, one of the first great paintings of a classical myth.
In Venice, Titian would become the master of rich colour, painting emperors and myths for some sixty years.
In the Ottoman world, Mimar Sinan would serve as chief architect for half a century, building the great mosques of Istanbul and Edirne.
Leonardo drew a man inside a circle and a square, the Vitruvian Man, a picture of ideal proportion.
Francis the First of France would grow into a king who loved Italian art, and brought Leonardo himself to France.
Hans Holbein the Younger would paint exact, piercing portraits at the court of Henry the Eighth.
In Milan, Leonardo painted The Last Supper on a monastery wall. His experimental paint soon began to flake.
In Rome, the young Michelangelo carved the Pieta, Mary holding her dead son, when he was barely in his twenties.
In the north, Hieronymus Bosch painted The Garden of Earthly Delights, from paradise to a nightmare hell, still puzzling scholars today.
Back in Florence, Leonardo began a portrait of a woman with a faint smile. The Mona Lisa is now the most visited painting on Earth.
Michelangelo carved his David from a single block of marble, and Florence took it as a symbol of its freedom.
Pope Julius began a new St Peter's in Rome. Bramante, Michelangelo and Bernini would all work on it.
Andrea Palladio was born in Padua. His villas and his books on architecture would shape buildings as far away as Britain and America.
In the Vatican, Raphael painted The School of Athens, with Plato and Aristotle at its heart, a picture of the whole age.
Giorgio Vasari would write the first history of art, and give this age its name, a rebirth.
After some four years on his back, Michelangelo finished the Sistine Chapel ceiling, with the creation of Adam at its heart.
In England, Thomas More imagined a perfect island society, and gave the world the word utopia.
In the Loire valley, Francis the First began Chambord, with a double spiral staircase perhaps designed by Leonardo, who died that year.
Pieter Bruegel would paint crowded village life and wintry landscapes like Hunters in the Snow.
In 1527 unpaid imperial soldiers sacked Rome, killing thousands and scattering its artists.
Five years later, Machiavelli's The Prince was finally published, after his death, and modern political thought began.
In France, Michel de Montaigne would invent the essay, writing honestly about himself and doubting easy answers.
Born on Crete and trained in Venice and Rome, El Greco carried the late Renaissance to Toledo in Spain, with his stretched figures and strange colours.
And in 1564, the year Michelangelo died, William Shakespeare was born in Stratford, bringing the age to its last great voice.
Three centuries of looking back to the ancients, and Europe never saw itself the same way again.
